flawed_step: Step 1 is justified: every 2-degenerate graph is 3-colorable by deleting a degree-at-most-2 vertex and extending a coloring greedily. Step 2 would need to claim that every triangle-free graph of maximum degree 4 is 2-degenerate (or otherwise force the same reduction). This is unjustified and false: the explicit 4-regular counterexample below is not 3-colorable.
counterexample: Let G have vertices 0,...,11 and neighborhoods N(0)={1,4,6,9}, N(1)={0,2,5,7}, N(2)={1,3,6,8}, N(3)={2,4,7,9}, N(4)={0,3,5,8}, N(5)={1,4,10,11}, N(6)={0,2,10,11}, N(7)={1,3,8,11}, N(8)={2,4,7,10}, N(9)={0,3,10,11}, N(10)={5,6,8,9}, N(11)={5,6,7,9}. These symmetric lists define a simple 4-regular graph, so Delta(G)=4. Checking the displayed lists, no two vertices within any N(v) are adjacent; hence no triangle can contain v, and G is triangle-free. To prove G is not 3-colorable, consider the 5-cycle 0-1-2-3-4-0. In any 3-coloring of this cycle, one color Z occurs once, at some vertex s, while the other four vertices, in cyclic order after s, have colors X,Y,X,Y. There are five cases. If s=0, vertices 5,6,9 are forced to Z,X,Y, so each of 10 and 11 sees all three colors. If s=1, vertices 5 and 6 are forced to Y and Z, so 10 and 11 are both forced to X; then 7 sees Z,Y,X at vertices 1,3,11. If s=2, vertices 6,7,8 are forced to Y,Z,X; consequently 10=Z and 11=X, after which 5 sees Y,Z,X. If s=3, vertices 9,7,8 are forced to X,Y,Z; consequently 10=Y and 11=Z, after which 5 sees X,Y,Z. If s=4, vertices 5,9,8 are forced to X,Z,Y, so 10 sees all three colors. Every case is impossible. Thus G is triangle-free, has maximum degree 4, and is not 3-colorable.
assessment_summary: The proof attempt stops at the first necessary unsupported strengthening from easy greedy-coloring conditions to the stated hypotheses. The explicit 12-vertex graph verifies that this is not merely a proof gap: it satisfies the hypotheses but has no proper 3-coloring.
